01.note: Rav had offended Rabbi Hanina bar Hama by not starting his Torah reading over when Rabbi Hanina came in, and for thirteen years Rav came to him on the eve of Yom Kippur to ask forgiveness, which Rabbi Hanina refused. Here the Gemara reveals the reason: Rabbi Hanina had seen in a dream that Rav was being hung on a palm tree, and he held as a tradition that such a dream means the man will become head of a yeshiva. He said that this showed Rav was destined to lead, so he would not be appeased, in order that Rav would go and study Torah in Babylonia.
01.why: The Gemara has asked how Rabbi Hanina could keep refusing forgiveness, when Rava taught that anyone who sets aside his own honor has all his sins pardoned. This explanation answers that his refusal served a purpose rather than a grudge.

people.name: Rabbi Hanina
people.about: Rabbi Hanina bar Hama, the Sage Rav offended and who would not be appeased for thirteen years.

people.name: Rav
people.about: The Sage who sought Rabbi Hanina's forgiveness; in Rabbi Hanina's dream he was hung on a palm tree.

terms.meaning: The leader of an academy of Torah study. The translation explains that Rabbi Hanina feared two such leaders could not hold office side by side, so Rav's leadership had to happen elsewhere.
The region of present-day Iraq, home to a large Jewish community and great academies; Rav and Rabbi Hanina were in the Land of Israel.

01.flag: The STORY segment holds only the Gemara's explanation of Rabbi Hanina's refusal; the incident itself (Rav's reading, the offense, the thirteen years of appeals) is in BEFORE segment [2] and should probably be part of the story.

02.note: Rabbi Yehuda recalled that Queen Helene had a sukka in Lod more than twenty cubits high, and the Elders went in and out of it without saying a word to her about it. The other Sages answered that this proves nothing: she was a woman, and women are exempt from the sukka. Rabbi Yehuda replied that she had seven sons, and moreover that she did everything only as the Sages directed.
02.why: A teaching holds that a sukka taller than twenty cubits is unfit, while Rabbi Yehuda allows one up to forty or fifty; the Gemara raises his precedent as an objection to how two later Sages explained that dispute.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who allows a very tall sukka and cites Queen Helene's sukka as proof.

people.name: Queen Helene
people.about: A queen whose sukka in Lod was over twenty cubits high; Rabbi Yehuda says she had seven sons and followed the Sages in everything.

terms.meaning: The temporary booth Jews live and eat in during the festival of Sukkot. Its size and height are set by law.
An ancient measure of length, roughly the length of a forearm, about half a meter.
The leading Sages of the time, whose silence Rabbi Yehuda takes as approval.

03.note: Minyamin, Rav Ashi's servant, got his shirt wet and spread it over the sukka to dry. Rav Ashi told him to take it down, so that people would not say they were roofing the sukka with something that can become ritually impure. Minyamin objected that anyone could see it was wet and only drying. Rav Ashi answered that he meant: take it down once it is dry.
03.why: The discussion is about decorations and cloths placed on or under a sukka's roofing, and Rav Ashi has just ruled on decorations spread at its sides; this incident shows his concern for how a cloth on the roof looks to onlookers.

people.name: Minyamin
people.about: Rav Ashi's servant, who spread his wet shirt on the sukka to dry.

people.name: Rav Ashi
people.about: Minyamin's master, who told him to take the shirt down.

terms.meaning: The sukka's roof must be made of plant material that grew from the ground and is not a finished object; a garment cannot serve as roofing.
In Jewish law, finished vessels and garments can become ritually impure; anything that can is unfit to roof a sukka.

04.note: Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna came to the house of the Exilarch, where Rav Nahman put them up in a sukka whose decorations hung four handbreadths below the roofing. They kept silent and said nothing. Rav Nahman asked them whether the Sages had taken back their ruling. They answered that they were on a mission for a mitzva, and so were exempt from the sukka altogether.
04.why: Rav Nahman had ruled that such a sukka is fit, while Rav Hisda and Rabba bar Rav Huna ruled it unfit; the story shows that their silence while staying in it was not a concession.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A Sage who held that a sukka with decorations four handbreadths below the roof is unfit.

people.name: Rabba bar Rav Huna
people.about: Rav Hisda's companion, who shared his view.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: In charge of the Exilarch's household, by the translation's account; he held such a sukka fit and lodged the two in it.

terms.meaning: The official head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, who kept a large household.
A measure of about the width of a palm, roughly 8 to 10 centimeters.

terms.term: On a mission for a mitzva
terms.meaning: Someone traveling to perform a religious duty is exempt from other duties, such as dwelling in a sukka, while doing so.

05.note: Rabbi Yehuda recalled a time of danger when he and others brought boards four handbreadths wide, roofed a porch with them and sat beneath them. The other Sages answered that this proves nothing, since what people do in a time of danger is no proof.
05.why: Rav and Shmuel disagree about which boards Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda were arguing over; this teaching, in which Rabbi Yehuda cites boards four handbreadths wide, supports Rav's version of their dispute.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: The Sage who allows boards four handbreadths wide as sukka roofing and recalls using them himself.

terms.meaning: A period of persecution. The translation explains that non-Jewish rulers had forbidden building a sukka, so it was disguised as an ordinary porch roof.
A measure of about the width of a palm, roughly 8 to 10 centimeters.

06.note: Rav Dimi, arriving from the Land of Israel, reported an incident from Tzippori: once people forgot to bring a Torah scroll to the synagogue before Shabbat began. The next day they found sheets already spread over posts along the way, used them as partitions, carried the scroll and read from it. The Gemara corrects the wording: they cannot have spread the sheets on Shabbat itself, so they must have found them already in place.
06.why: The Gemara has argued that Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Yosei each accept hanging partitions only in limited cases, neither for Shabbat carrying; so it asks whose view Tzippori followed, and answers Rabbi Yishmael son of Rabbi Yosei.

people.name: Rav Dimi
people.about: A Sage who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia and reported the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Yishmael, son of Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage on whose authority, the Gemara says, the people of Tzippori acted.

terms.meaning: Jewish law forbids carrying objects on Shabbat in open areas unless they are enclosed by partitions, which is why the sheets mattered.
A wall that hangs from above without reaching the ground, like a sheet on posts. The Sages dispute when it counts as a real wall.

07.note: Reish Lakish, about to quote a ruling of Rabbi Hiyya and his sons, first honored them: 'I am the atonement for Rabbi Hiyya and his sons.' When Torah was forgotten in the Land of Israel, he said, Ezra came up from Babylonia and reestablished it; when it was forgotten again, Hillel the Babylonian came up and reestablished it; and when it was forgotten yet again, Rabbi Hiyya and his sons came up and reestablished it. He then cited their ruling that Rabbi Dosa and the Sages did not disagree about the soft mats of Usha.
07.why: Reish Lakish had just explained a disputed word as meaning ordinary mats; the Gemara shows he is consistent, since he cites Rabbi Hiyya and his sons on which mats Rabbi Dosa and the Sages argued over.

people.name: Reish Lakish
people.about: The Sage who praises Rabbi Hiyya and his sons and quotes their ruling.

people.name: Rabbi Hiyya
people.about: A Sage who, with his sons, came up from Babylonia and restored forgotten Torah, in Reish Lakish's account.

people.name: Ezra
people.about: Came up from Babylonia and reestablished the forgotten Torah, the first of the three in Reish Lakish's list.

people.name: Hillel the Babylonian
people.about: Came up from Babylonia and reestablished the Torah when it was forgotten a second time.

terms.meaning: A phrase of deep respect, roughly 'may I suffer in their place', said before quoting someone greatly honored.
Soft mats made in the town of Usha for lying on; because they are made for use, they can become ritually impure.

07.flag: Ends mid-sentence: Rabbi Hiyya's ruling on the mats of Usha continues into AFTER segment [5]. The passage is also more a statement of praise than a narrated story.

08.note: Rabbi Hananya recalled that when he went down to Babylonia, he met an Elder who told him that one may roof a sukka with a mat. When he came back to his uncle, Rabbi Yehoshua, and told him, Rabbi Yehoshua agreed. Rav Hisda added that this holds only for a mat without an upturned edge.
08.why: The discussion is whether various mats count as vessels that can become ritually impure, which would make them unfit as sukka roofing; this report allows a mat, and Rav Hisda limits it to one that is not a vessel.

people.name: Rabbi Hananya
people.about: The nephew of Rabbi Yehoshua, who heard the ruling from an Elder in Babylonia.

people.name: Rabbi Yehoshua
people.about: Rabbi Hananya's father's brother, who agreed with the Elder's ruling.

people.name: Rav Hisda
people.about: A later Sage who limits the ruling to mats without an upturned edge.

terms.meaning: Babylonia, home of the largest Jewish community outside the Land of Israel.
A raised rim that turns a flat mat into a container, which can become ritually impure and so cannot roof a sukka.

09.note: Rabbi Shimon recalled an incident involving Tavi, the slave of Rabban Gamliel, who slept under a bed in the sukka. By the translation's account, Rabban Gamliel remarked that Tavi did so because he was a Torah scholar and knew that slaves are exempt from the sukka. Rabbi Shimon said that from Rabban Gamliel's conversation they learned two things: that slaves are exempt from the sukka, and that one who sleeps under a bed in the sukka has not fulfilled his obligation.
09.why: The mishna disputes whether sleeping under a bed inside a sukka counts; Rabbi Yehuda says it does, and Rabbi Shimon cites Tavi's case to show it does not, since a bed is like a tent that blocks the roofing.

people.name: Tavi
people.about: Rabban Gamliel's slave, who slept under a bed in the sukka.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Tavi's master, whose remark about him taught two laws.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon
people.about: The Sage who reports the incident and what it teaches.

terms.meaning: A non-Jewish slave in a Jewish household, who keeps only some commandments and is exempt from the sukka.
Properly performed the commandment, here dwelling under the sukka's roof.

09.flag: The incident's events (Tavi sleeping under the bed, Rabban Gamliel's remark) appear only in the translation's explanatory gloss; the mishna's own telling, at Sukkah 20b, is not included.

10.note: Rabban Gamliel and Rabbi Akiva were traveling together on a ship, and Rabbi Akiva built a sukka on the deck. The next day the wind blew and tore it away. Rabban Gamliel said to him: 'Akiva, where is your sukka?' The text does not give Rabbi Akiva's reply.
10.why: Rabban Gamliel rules a sukka on a ship unfit and Rabbi Akiva rules it fit; the mishna follows Rabbi Akiva, and Abaye explains they disagree over whether a sukka must withstand a sea wind.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Rabbi Akiva's traveling companion, who held a sukka on a ship unfit.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Built a sukka on the ship, holding it fit.

terms.meaning: The temporary booth Jews live and eat in during the festival of Sukkot.

11.note: When people brought Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai a cooked dish to taste, and brought Rabban Gamliel two dates and a bucket of water, each said: take them up to the sukka. In contrast, when they gave Rabbi Tzadok less than an egg-bulk of food, he took it in a cloth, ate it outside the sukka, and said no blessing after it.
11.why: The prior mishna allows a snack outside the sukka; the Gemara says this one teaches that a person may be stricter. It then infers from Rabbi Tzadok that an egg-bulk would need a sukka, against Rav Yosef and Abaye, and rejects the inference.

people.name: Rabban Yohanan ben Zakkai
people.about: Was brought a cooked dish to taste and had it taken to the sukka.

people.name: Rabban Gamliel
people.about: Was brought two dates and a bucket of water and had them taken to the sukka.

people.name: Rabbi Tzadok
people.about: Ate less than an egg-bulk of food outside the sukka, holding it in a cloth.

terms.meaning: The volume of an egg, a standard minimum measure for food in Jewish law.
The thanks recited after a meal; the translation explains Rabbi Tzadok held it is not required for so small an amount.

11.flag: Starts mid-sentence: the first incident's opening (the dish and the dates being brought) is in BEFORE segment [3].

12.note: Rabbi Elai went to greet his teacher, Rabbi Eliezer, in Lod on the Festival. Rabbi Eliezer said to him: 'Elai, you are not one of those who rest on the Festival.' For Rabbi Eliezer used to say: 'I praise the lazy, who do not leave their houses on the Festival,' since it is written, 'You shall rejoice, you and your household.'
12.why: The Gemara sets this against Rabbi Yitzhak's teaching that one must greet one's teacher on a Festival, and reconciles them: the duty applies when one can go and return the same day, and Rabbi Eliezer's objection when one cannot.

people.name: Rabbi Elai
people.about: A student who went to greet his teacher on the Festival.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: Rabbi Elai's teacher in Lod, who held that people should stay home on the Festival.

terms.meaning: One of the pilgrimage holidays, here Sukkot, when people traditionally rejoiced at home with their families.
The translation explains this word in the verse as one's wife; one who is away cannot rejoice with her.

13.note: Rabbi Eliezer was staying in the Upper Galilee in the sukka of Yohanan son of Rabbi Elai when the sun began to shine into the sukka. Yohanan asked whether he might spread a sheet over it, and Rabbi Eliezer answered only that every tribe of Israel produced a judge. When the sun reached the middle of the sukka he asked again, and Rabbi Eliezer said every tribe produced prophets, and Judah and Benjamin set up kings by prophets' word. When the sun reached Rabbi Eliezer's feet, Yohanan spread a sheet, and Rabbi Eliezer threw his cloak over his shoulder and left. The Gemara comments that he never said anything he had not heard from his teacher.
13.why: One of several stories about Rabbi Eliezer on Sukkot; the Gemara then asks how he could stay in someone else's sukka, given his own rulings, and concludes it was Shabbat and Yohanan's question was about building on Shabbat.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: The guest who would not answer a question he had not heard ruled on by his teacher.

people.name: Yohanan, son of Rabbi Elai
people.about: Rabbi Eliezer's host, who asked whether he could spread a sheet against the sun.

terms.term: Spreading a sheet over the sukka
terms.meaning: Adding a cover to a structure; the question is whether this counts as forbidden building or as adding to a temporary tent.
The hilly northern part of the Land of Israel.

14.note: While Rabbi Eliezer stayed in the Upper Galilee, people asked him thirty laws about the sukka. To twelve he answered that he had heard a ruling, and to eighteen that he had not; Rabbi Yosei son of Rabbi Yehuda says it was the reverse. They asked whether everything he said came only from what he had heard. He answered that they had now forced him to say something he had not heard from his teachers: no one ever came into the study hall before him, he never slept there, never left anyone behind there, never engaged in idle talk, and never said anything he had not heard from his teacher.
14.why: The previous story ended with the Gemara saying Rabbi Eliezer never said anything he had not heard from his teacher; this similar incident shows that habit in his own words.

people.name: Rabbi Eliezer
people.about: A Sage asked thirty questions about the sukka, who answered only what he had heard from his teachers.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei, son of Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Gives the reverse count: eighteen heard and twelve not.

terms.meaning: Rules of Jewish law; here, questions about the laws of the sukka.
The house of study where Sages and students learned Torah together.

15.note: When the daughter-in-law of Shammai the Elder gave birth, Shammai broke away the plaster of the roof, leaving the beams, and roofed over the bed so that the newborn would be under a sukka roof.
15.why: The mishna exempts small children who still need their mother; the Gemara asks whether the incident contradicts this, and answers that the mishna is incomplete: Shammai was strict even for infants, and this is an example.

people.name: Shammai the Elder
people.about: The Sage who roofed over his newborn grandchild's bed.

terms.meaning: A child below the age of religious obligation. The mishna obligates only a child who no longer needs his mother in the sukka.
The layer of plaster over the roof beams; with it removed, the beams could serve as sukka roofing.

16.note: Abaye was sitting before Rav Yosef in the sukka when the wind blew and brought splinters down from the roofing. Rav Yosef told the household to clear his things out of there. Abaye objected that the mishna says one leaves only when rain would spoil a congealed dish. Rav Yosef answered that for him, since he is delicate, this was as bad as a spoiled congealed dish.
16.why: The mishna says one may leave the sukka in rain hard enough to spoil a congealed dish; Rav Yosef's reply shows the measure depends on the person, so discomfort that bothers a delicate person counts.

people.name: Abaye
people.about: Rav Yosef's student, who questioned him for leaving the sukka.

people.name: Rav Yosef
people.about: Abaye's teacher, who called himself delicate and left the sukka when splinters fell.

terms.meaning: A thick porridge that even a little rain ruins; the mishna uses it to measure when rain is heavy enough to leave the sukka.

17.note: Rabbi Yohanan, in the name of Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai, explained the verse 'For I the Lord love justice, I hate robbery in a burnt-offering' with a parable. A human king passing a customs house told his servants to pay the tax to the tax collectors. They asked: doesn't all the tax belong to you? He answered that all travelers would learn from him and not evade the tax. So too, God says He hates robbery in a burnt-offering, so that His children will learn from Him and keep away from robbery.
17.why: The Gemara has ruled that a stolen animal cannot be offered, even once it legally belongs to the robber, since a mitzva may not be done by means of a sin; this teaching on a verse about robbery and offerings follows.

people.name: Rabbi Yohanan
people.about: The Sage who reports this teaching.

people.name: Rabbi Shimon ben Yohai
people.about: The Sage in whose name the teaching is given.

people.name: The Holy One, Blessed be He
people.about: God, who in the parable's lesson hates robbery so His children will learn from Him.

terms.meaning: A Temple sacrifice burned entirely on the altar.
A toll station where travelers paid tax on goods passing through.

18.note: An old woman came before Rav Nahman and said that the Exilarch and all the Sages of his house were sitting in a stolen sukka. The translation explains she claimed the Exilarch's servants had stolen her wood to build it. She screamed, but Rav Nahman paid her no attention. She said: a woman whose father had three hundred and eighteen slaves is screaming before you, and you pay her no attention? Rav Nahman told the Sages that she was a screamer, and that she had a right only to the value of the wood.
18.why: The Gemara has just said that everyone agrees a person who builds a sukka from stolen wood owes the owner only the wood's value; Rav Nahman's ruling applies exactly that principle.

people.name: Rav Nahman
people.about: The judge before whom the old woman complained.

people.name: The Exilarch
people.about: The head of the Jewish community in Babylonia, accused of sitting in a sukka made of her wood.

terms.meaning: The official head of the Jewish community in Babylonia.
The number of servants Abraham led into battle in Genesis; the translation explains that she is claiming honor as a descendant of Abraham.

19.note: Rabbi Yosei recalled an incident in which Rabbi Akiva came to the synagogue with his etrog so large he carried it on his shoulder. Rabbi Yehuda answered: is that a proof? There too, the Sages told him, 'That is not beauty.'
19.why: The mishna disputes the maximum size of an etrog: Rabbi Yehuda says one must be able to hold two in one hand, while Rabbi Yosei allows one so large it needs both hands; Rabbi Yosei cites Rabbi Akiva's etrog as his proof.

people.name: Rabbi Yosei
people.about: The Sage who allows a very large etrog and tells the incident.

people.name: Rabbi Akiva
people.about: Brought an etrog to the synagogue so large he carried it on his shoulder.

people.name: Rabbi Yehuda
people.about: Disputes Rabbi Yosei, saying the Sages told Rabbi Akiva his etrog was not beautiful.

terms.meaning: A citron, a lemon-like fruit, one of the four species held on Sukkot.
The Torah calls the etrog the fruit of a beautiful tree, so an etrog that is not beautiful is unfit.

20.note: Rabbi Meir recalled that the prominent residents of Jerusalem used to bind their lulavs with gold rings. The Sages answered that this proves nothing: they bound them underneath with their own species.
20.why: The mishna disputes what may bind the lulav: Rabbi Yehuda says only its own species, Rabbi Meir says even a cord; Rabbi Meir offers Jerusalem's custom as proof, and the Sages explain the gold was only decoration.

people.name: Rabbi Meir
people.about: The Sage who allows binding the lulav with anything and cites the Jerusalem custom.

terms.meaning: A palm branch, held on Sukkot bound together with myrtle and willow branches.
Material from one of the four species of Sukkot, such as palm fibers, rather than an outside material.
